steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on CP-MAE, a masked-autoencoder approach to de-identifying 3D MRI scans by remodeling the face. Cover the privacy problem, existing de-identification methods and their trade-off, why MAEs instead of GANs, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Privacy problem: faces can be rendered from MRI scans
- Existing de-identification methods and their trade-off
- Remodeling paradigm (CP-GAN)
- Masked autoencoders as an alternative to GANs
- Contributions (CP-MAE)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Privacy problem
  - MRI usually shown as 2D slices, but 3D model renderable (volumetric raytracing) -> realistic face
  - attacker with face database + identities finds closest match -> may infer identity
- Existing methods
  - many de-identification methods over the years; mostly simple, differ in aggressiveness
  - FACE MASK (cite): blurs the face; skull-stripping, e.g. MRI WATERSHED (cite): keep only brain
  - medical tools need certain landmarks; if absent, analysis impaired or impossible (cite)
  - not aggressive enough -> identity still inferable; harmful when automatic, no oversight, large corpus
- Remodeling
  - CP-GAN (cite), GAN-based: remodel face, keep medically-relevant info
  - copy brain, remodel rest so it "looks like" a real scan but no info on real face/identity
  - removes trade-off: landmarks placed accurately, minimal domain shift -> safer, more effective
- MAEs
  - recently propelled generative approaches; predict stochastically-masked segments, no adversarial game
  - advantages: (i) training stability, (ii) data efficiency
  - MRI de-identification: high memory, data scarcity, instability from small batches -> MAEs attractive
- Contributions
  - CP-MAE for high-res MRI; previous remodeling limited to 128^{3}, now 256^{3}, 8-fold more voxels
  - first to combine volumetric VQ-VAE with MAE for 3D MR image synthesis
  - superior de-identification; trains robustly on modest datasets (ADNI, OASIS-3)
  - minimal effect on brain tissue and subcortical segmentation

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
MRI scans are usually visualized as 2D slices, but it is also possible to render a high-quality 3D model with techniques like volumetric raytracing, and this gives a realistic depiction of the patient's face. This is a problem for data privacy: given an MRI scan and a face database with the associated identities, a malicious actor can find the closest match to the face rendering, and so they can potentially infer the identity of the patient.

Over the years various de-identification methods have appeared that remove the privacy-sensitive parts. Most of them are quite simple and they differ in how aggressive they are. FACE MASK only blurs out the face, while skull-stripping methods like MRI WATERSHED keep only the brain and remove everything else. But these traditional approaches can be problematic. Many tools in the medical workflow need certain landmarks to be present as preconditions. If the landmarks are missing, the analysis might be impaired or in the worst case it might be impossible to do the analysis at all. On the other hand, if a method is not aggressive enough it might still be possible to infer the identity of the patient, and this is especially harmful when the tool is used automatically and without oversight on a large corpus of scans.

- CP-GAN (recent, GAN-based): remodel face, keep medically-relevant info; copy brain, remodel rest so it "looks like" a real scan; accurate landmarks, minimal domain shift
- MAEs: predict stochastically-masked segments instead of adversarial game; (i) training stability, (ii) data efficiency; fit MRI setting (memory, data scarcity, small batches)
- Contributions:
  1. CP-MAE for high-res MRI: 128^{3} -> 256^{3}, 8-fold more voxels
  2. first to combine volumetric VQ-VAE with MAE for 3D MR synthesis
  3. better de-identification, robust on modest datasets (ADNI, OASIS-3)
  4. minimal effect on brain tissue and subcortical segmentation

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
MRI scans are usually visualized as 2D slices, but it is also possible to render a high-quality 3D model with techniques like volumetric raytracing, and this gives a realistic depiction of the patient's face. This is a problem for data privacy: given an MRI scan and a face database with the associated identities, a malicious actor can find the closest match to the face rendering, and so they can potentially infer the identity of the patient.

Over the years various de-identification methods have appeared that remove the privacy-sensitive parts. Most of them are quite simple and they differ in how aggressive they are. FACE MASK only blurs out the face, while skull-stripping methods like MRI WATERSHED keep only the brain and remove everything else. But these traditional approaches can be problematic. Many tools in the medical workflow need certain landmarks to be present as preconditions. If the landmarks are missing, the analysis might be impaired or in the worst case it might be impossible to do the analysis at all. On the other hand, if a method is not aggressive enough it might still be possible to infer the identity of the patient, and this is especially harmful when the tool is used automatically and without oversight on a large corpus of scans.

A GAN-based approach called CP-GAN was proposed recently and it introduced a new paradigm, which is to remodel the face and leave the medically-relevant information intact. Basically the MRI scan of a patient is de-identified by copying the brain and remodeling the other parts so that they "look like" they belong to an actual MRI scan, but they do not give away information about the real face (or identity) of the patient. This approach removes the trade-off mentioned above, because it makes sure landmarks are placed accurately and so minimizes domain shift, which leads to safer and more effective de-identification.

Recently masked autoencoders (MAEs) have appeared and pushed generative approaches forward. They depart from the GAN methodology that was dominant before, because they predict stochastically-masked segments of the data instead of formulating an adversarial game. MAEs have two fundamental advantages over GANs: (i) higher training stability and (ii) higher data efficiency. MRI de-identification with generative models has high memory requirements and data scarcity, and it often suffers from instability because of small batch sizes, so MAEs look like an attractive alternative.

In this work we adapt masked autoencoders for MRI de-identification. Our contributions are:

1. We propose CP-MAE, a model based on a masked autoencoder that can deal with high-resolution MRI scans. Previous remodeling-based methods were limited to a resolution of 128^{3}, but our model can produce de-identified scans of size 256^{3}, which is an 8-fold increase in the number of voxels.

2. As far as we know, our model is the first to combine a volumetric VQ-VAE with an MAE for 3D MR image synthesis.

3. We show that CP-MAE has better de-identification performance than other methods and that it can be trained robustly on modestly-sized datasets (e.g., ADNI, OASIS-3).

4. We show that de-identification with CP-MAE has minimal effects on brain tissue and subcortical segmentation tasks compared to other approaches.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
While MRI scans are usually visualized as 2D slices, it is also possible to render a high-quality 3D model using techniques such as volumetric raytracing, which yields a realistic depiction of a patient's face. This is problematic in terms of data privacy: given an MRI scan and a face database with associated identities, a malicious actor can find the closest match to a given face rendering, which allows them to potentially infer a patient's identity.

Various de-identification methods that address the removal of privacy-sensitive parts have appeared over the years. Most are quite simple and differ in their level of aggressiveness: while FACE MASK [1] merely blurs out the face, skull-stripping methods such as MRI WATERSHED [2] retain only the brain and remove everything else. However, these traditional approaches are potentially problematic. Simply put, many tools in the medical workflow require the presence of certain landmarks as preconditions. If those landmarks are absent, the analysis might be impaired or, in the worst case, impossible to perform at all [3]. On the other hand, if a method is not aggressive enough it might still be feasible to infer a patient's identity, which is especially harmful when such a tool is used automatically and without oversight on a large corpus of scans.

A recently proposed GAN-based approach named CP-GAN [4] introduced a new paradigm: remodel the face and leave the medically-relevant information intact. Simply put, a patient's MRI scan is de-identified by copying their brain and remodeling the remaining parts so that they "look like" they belong to an actual MRI scan but do not give away information about the patient's real face (or identity). This approach eliminates the aforementioned trade-off, as it ensures accurate placement of landmarks and thus minimizes domain shift, leading to safer and more effective de-identification.

Recently, the emergence of masked autoencoders (MAEs) has propelled generative approaches forward, departing from the previously dominant GAN methodology by predicting stochastically-masked segments of the data instead of formulating an adversarial game.

MAEs offer two fundamental advantages over GANs: (i) higher training stability, and (ii) higher data efficiency. Since MRI de-identification with generative models involves high memory requirements and data scarcity, and often suffers from instability due to small batch sizes, MAEs appear to be an attractive alternative.

In this work, we adapt masked autoencoders for MRI de-identification. Our contributions are as follows:

1. We propose CP-MAE, a masked autoencoder-based model that can deal with high-resolution MRI scans. Whereas previous remodeling-based methods were limited to a resolution of 128^{3}, our model can produce de-identified scans of size 256^{3}, an 8-fold increase in the number of voxels.

2. To the best of our knowledge, our model is the first to combine a volumetric VQ-VAE with an MAE for 3D MR image synthesis.

3. We demonstrate that CP-MAE has superior de-identification performance compared to other methods and can be robustly trained on modestly-sized datasets (e.g., ADNI, OASIS-3).

4. We show that de-identification with CP-MAE introduces minimal effects on brain tissue and subcortical segmentation tasks compared to other approaches.
